topic.title: Blood components, cell lysis and blood vessels
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Blood opens the B2 Foundation paper more often than not: Summer 2025 Q1 was 7 marks (three components matched to functions [3], then nucleus, biconcave, iron and a plasma substance [1] each) and Summer 2024 Q2 was 5 marks. Vessels come back later in the same paper attached to the heart — Summer 2025 Higher Q1(b) asked for two vessel types and only [1] of the [2] was usually earned. Summer 2022 Higher Q1(b) was a five-row tick table on vessel features worth [6]. Cell lysis is Higher only and has appeared in Unit 7 Booklet B.
mustMemorise: Red cells: biconcave, no nucleus, haemoglobin containing iron — they carry oxygen
White cells: defence against disease. Platelets: convert fibrinogen to fibrin, so blood clots and a scab forms
Plasma transports cells, food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea — not oxygen
Artery: thick wall with muscle and elastic fibres, small lumen, high pressure, away from the heart
Vein: thin wall, large lumen, low pressure, towards the heart, valves prevent backflow
Capillary: wall one cell thick and permeable, for exchange with the tissues
Higher: red blood cells in water take in water by osmosis and burst — lysis
Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size, in the same unit
notOnThisSpec: The clotting cascade beyond fibrinogen to fibrin
Arterioles, venules and the structure of the three wall layers by name

note.title: Blood components, cell lysis and blood vessels
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Red cells carry oxygen; white cells defend; platelets clot; plasma transports
Plasma carries food, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea — oxygen goes in the red cells
Artery: thick wall, small lumen. Vein: thin wall, large lumen, valves. Capillary: one cell thick, permeable
Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size, both in the same unit

mustBeAbleTo: Name the four components of blood from a smear and give the function of each
Give three adaptations of a red blood cell, each a different idea
Name substances the plasma transports, and know that oxygen is not one of them
Say what platelets do, in the specification's words: convert fibrinogen to fibrin
Describe an artery, a vein and a capillary by wall thickness, muscle and elastic fibres, lumen and valves
Relate each of those features to the vessel's job
Explain why veins have valves and arteries do not
Higher Tier: explain what happens to red blood cells in pure water, and why it differs from a plant cell
Calculate a magnification, converting both lengths to the same unit first
Work out a lumen width, a percentage of a volume and a ratio from counts
sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Blood often opens the Foundation paper, with a matching exercise worth [3] and then single [1] recall lines — nucleus, biconcave, iron, a substance in the plasma. Vessels appear both on their own (a tick table worth up to [6]) and attached to the heart question, where naming the vessel type is [1] each. Cell lysis is Higher only. The accept lists are tight: 'biconcave' not 'round', 'capillary' not 'small vein'.
traps: Not linking platelets to both of their functions (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q1)
Giving 'round' or 'flat' instead of 'biconcave' (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q1)
Being unable to give the function or the adaptations of a red blood cell (Summer 2024 B2 Foundation Q2)
Giving oxygen as a substance transported by the plasma (Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q2)
Naming a function of a component when the question asks what the plasma carries (Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q2)
Not naming the vessel of exchange as a capillary (Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q1)
Swapping the artery's and the vein's wall thickness and lumen size
Calling a red blood cell in water 'turgid' instead of burst (Summer 2023 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q4)
Dividing millimetres by micrometres in a magnification

workedExamples.stem:
The table gives measurements from a stained section of an artery and a vein that were the same width on the outside.
(a) Calculate the width of the lumen of the artery. [2]
(b) Explain how the artery's wall suits the job it does. [2]

data.caption: Two vessels of the same outside width, measured from a stained section

steps.decision: The wall runs all the way round, so it is crossed twice on the way through. Subtracting it once is the classic slip here.
Outside width minus the two wall thicknesses. Compare it with the vein's 5.0 mm lumen: same tube from outside, very different inside.

options: Because the wall is crossed once on the way in and once on the way out
Because the artery wall is thicker than the vein wall
Because the lumen is always half the outside width
whyMenu.explain: A cross-section is a ring: the outside width contains two thicknesses of wall plus the lumen.

steps.working: The wall is thick, with muscle and elastic fibres in it.
steps.decision: Name the structure first. 'Thick' on its own is a description; the fibres are what the scheme lists.

steps.working: It has to withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart, and the elastic fibres let it stretch and recoil with each beat.
steps.decision: Then the reason. Structure plus function: the function is where the mark is.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 3.0 mm. (b) The wall is thick and contains muscle and elastic fibres, so it can withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart and can stretch and recoil with every beat.

twin.stem: A capillary is 0.008 mm wide on the outside and its wall is 0.001 mm thick. Calculate the width of its lumen, in mm.

workedExamples.stem:
A drawing of one red blood cell measures 42 mm across. A real red blood cell is 7 µm across.
(a) Calculate the magnification of the drawing. [3]
(b) Give two ways the cell is adapted to carry oxygen. [2]

steps.decision: Both lengths must be in the same unit before you divide, and micrometres are the smaller one, so convert the drawing. There are 1000 µm in 1 mm.
Drawn over real, in that order. Turning it upside down gives a number smaller than 1, which is a warning sign in itself.
A magnification has no unit: it is a ratio of two lengths. Write it with a multiplication sign in front.

steps.working: It is a biconcave disc, which gives it a large surface area for absorbing oxygen.
steps.decision: Adaptation plus its reason. 'Biconcave' alone usually earns the mark, but the reason makes the answer safe.

steps.working: It has no nucleus, so there is more room inside it for haemoglobin.
steps.decision: The second adaptation must be a different idea from the first, not a rewording of it.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) ×6000. (b) It is a biconcave disc, which gives a large surface area for absorbing oxygen, and it has no nucleus, so there is more room for haemoglobin.

items.stem: Before we start, three things you have already met. Which structure is found in an animal cell but NOT in a bacterial cell?

options.text: a nucleus
options.feedback: A nucleus. Keep hold of it: one blood cell is famous for giving its nucleus up.

options.text: a cell membrane
options.feedback: Bacteria have a membrane too. What they lack is a nucleus; their DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm.

options.text: cytoplasm
options.feedback: Every cell has cytoplasm.

options.text: a cell wall
options.feedback: Bacteria do have a wall, though not a cellulose one. Animal cells are the ones without.

items.stem: A cell is put into pure water. Which way does water move?

options.text: into the cell
options.feedback: Into the cell: pure water is the most dilute solution there is.

options.text: out of the cell
options.feedback: Water moves towards the more concentrated solution, and that is the cytoplasm inside the cell.

options.text: neither way
options.feedback: There is no net movement only when the two solutions match. Pure water and cytoplasm do not.

options.text: into the cell, using energy from respiration
options.feedback: The direction is right, but osmosis is free: it needs no energy.

options.text: Molecules spreading from where there are more of them to where there are fewer
options.feedback: Down the gradient. Every exchange in a capillary works this way.

options.text: Molecules being pumped using energy
options.feedback: That is active transport. Diffusion costs nothing.

options.text: Water moving through a membrane
options.feedback: That is osmosis, which is one special case of diffusion.

options.text: Blood being pushed along a vessel
options.feedback: That is the heart's doing, not diffusion.

items.stem: Which component of blood converts fibrinogen to fibrin?
items.skill: Match a component to its function

options.text: platelets
options.feedback: Platelets. Fibrin makes the mesh that traps cells and forms a clot, and then a scab.

options.text: red blood cells
options.feedback: Red cells carry oxygen. Clotting is the platelets' job.

options.text: white blood cells
options.feedback: White cells defend against disease. Summer 2025 examiners recorded that many candidates could not link platelets to their two functions.

options.text: plasma
options.feedback: Plasma is the liquid that carries everything. It contains the fibrinogen, but the platelets do the converting.

items.stem: Which of these is an adaptation of a red blood cell for carrying oxygen?

options.text: It has no nucleus, so there is more room for haemoglobin
options.feedback: No nucleus, more haemoglobin. Summer 2024 examiners found the adaptations surprisingly poorly known.

options.text: It has a large nucleus to control oxygen uptake
options.feedback: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus at all — that is the point.

options.text: It is a cube, which packs tightly in the vessel
options.feedback: It is a biconcave disc: dimpled on both sides, which gives a large surface area.

options.text: It contains fibrin to help it stick to the vessel wall
options.feedback: Fibrin belongs to clotting. A red cell contains haemoglobin.

items.stem: Which substance does blood plasma transport?

options.text: urea
options.feedback: Urea, on its way to the kidneys. Plasma also carries cells, food molecules, carbon dioxide and hormones.

options.text: oxygen
options.feedback: Almost all the oxygen travels inside red blood cells, bound to haemoglobin. Summer 2023 examiners saw oxygen given here and it was not credited.

options.text: haemoglobin
options.feedback: Haemoglobin stays inside the red blood cells; it is not dissolved in the plasma.

options.text: fibrin
options.feedback: Fibrin only forms when a clot is made. Plasma carries the fibrinogen it is made from.

items.stem: Why does an artery have a much smaller lumen than a vein of the same outside width?

options.text: Its wall is far thicker, to withstand high pressure
options.feedback: The wall takes up the space. Thick muscle and elastic fibres are what high-pressure blood needs.

options.text: It carries less blood than a vein
options.feedback: The same blood passes through both. The difference is the wall, not the amount.

options.text: It has valves that take up room
options.feedback: Arteries have no valves. Veins are the ones with valves.

options.text: It is further from the heart
options.feedback: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and the pressure there is high, which is why the wall is thick.

items.stem: Why is a capillary wall only one cell thick?

options.text: So materials can be exchanged quickly with the tissues
options.feedback: Short distance, fast diffusion. Exchange is the whole job of a capillary.

options.text: So the blood can travel faster
options.feedback: Blood actually flows slowly in capillaries, which gives more time for exchange.

options.text: So it can withstand high pressure
options.feedback: A thin wall is the opposite of what withstands pressure. That is the artery's problem.

options.text: So valves can open and close inside it
options.feedback: Capillaries have no valves. Only veins do.

items.stem: Higher Tier. Red blood cells are placed in pure water. What happens, and why?
items.skill: Apply osmosis to an animal cell

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cells burst
options.feedback: Lysis. With no cell wall there is nothing to limit the water entering.

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cells become turgid
options.feedback: Turgid is a plant-cell word: it needs a wall for the contents to press against.

options.text: Water leaves by osmosis and the cells shrink
options.feedback: That happens in a concentrated salt solution. Pure water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, so water moves in.

options.text: Nothing happens, because the cells have no nucleus
options.feedback: The missing nucleus makes no difference to osmosis. The missing cell wall makes all the difference.

parts.workedSolution: They defend the body against disease.

parts.stem: State the function of the platelets.

accepted: they convert fibrinogen to fibrin, so the blood clots

scheme.for: convert fibrinogen to fibrin / cause blood clotting

parts.workedSolution: They convert fibrinogen to fibrin, which makes the blood clot and a scab form.

parts.stem: Name one substance, apart from blood cells, that the plasma transports.

scheme.for: any one of: food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones, urea

parts.workedSolution: Urea. Food molecules, carbon dioxide and hormones are all credited too.

parts.stem: Give three ways a red blood cell is adapted to carry oxygen. Write a different adaptation on each line.

accepted: it is a biconcave disc, it has no nucleus, and it is packed with haemoglobin

scheme.for: biconcave shape (giving a large surface area)

parts.stem: Name the vessel that carries blood away from the heart under high pressure.
parts.workedSolution: An artery.

parts.stem: Name the vessel with valves that carries blood back towards the heart under low pressure.
parts.workedSolution: A vein.

parts.stem: Name the vessel whose permeable wall is one cell thick, where materials are exchanged with the tissues.
parts.workedSolution: A capillary.

commonErrors.feedback: Arteries and veins have thick multi-layered walls. The one-cell-thick vessel where exchange happens is the capillary. Summer 2025 examiners recorded that fewer candidates could name it than could describe what it does.

context.setting: Measurements from a stained section of an artery

data.caption: Two vessels of the same outside width, measured from a stained section

parts.stem: The artery is 6.0 mm across the outside and its wall is 1.5 mm thick. Calculate the width of its lumen, in mm.
hints: The wall goes all the way round, so how many thicknesses lie across the vessel?
parts.workedSolution: The wall is crossed twice, so it accounts for 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 mm. The lumen is 6.0 − 3.0 = 3.0 mm.

commonErrors.feedback: The wall has been subtracted once. A cross-section is a ring, so the outside width contains two thicknesses of wall plus the lumen.

context.setting: A drawing made from a blood smear

parts.stem: A student's drawing of a red blood cell measures 42 mm across. The real cell is 7 µm across. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
hints: Put both lengths in the same unit first. There are 1000 µm in 1 mm.
parts.workedSolution: 42 mm is 42000 µm. Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size = 42000 ÷ 7 = ×6000. A magnification is a ratio, so it carries no unit.

commonErrors.feedback: Millimetres have been divided by micrometres. Convert the drawing to micrometres first: 1 mm is 1000 µm.
Real size has been divided by drawn size. Magnification is drawn ÷ real, and a magnified drawing always gives a number bigger than one.

context.setting: One field of view of a stained blood smear

parts.stem: In one field of view a student counted 240 red blood cells and 3 white blood cells. How many times more red cells than white cells were there?
hints: Divide the larger count by the smaller one.
parts.workedSolution: 240 ÷ 3 = 80 times as many.

commonErrors.feedback: The counts have been divided the wrong way round. 'How many times more red cells' means red divided by white.

parts.stem: Red blood cells are placed in distilled water. Describe and explain what happens to them.

accepted: water enters the cells by osmosis because the distilled water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, the cells swell, and because they have no cell wall to limit the water entering they burst

parts.workedSolution: Distilled water is more dilute than the cytoplasm inside the red blood cells, so water moves into them by osmosis through their selectively permeable membranes. The cells swell, and because an animal cell has no cell wall to limit the entry of water, they keep swelling until the membrane splits and they burst. This is called lysis.

indicativeContent.point: an artery has a thick wall containing muscle and elastic fibres
which withstands the high pressure of blood carried away from the heart, and stretches and recoils with each beat
an artery has a small lumen; a vein has a large one
a vein has a thin wall with little muscle, because blood in it is at low pressure
a vein has valves, which prevent backflow and keep the blood moving towards the heart

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Answers that list features without saying what each one is for cap at Band B: the specification asks for structures related to functions. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Three vessels, and for each one a structure and the job it suits — that is six points already.
The words that lift an answer to Band A are lumen, elastic fibres, valves, backflow and permeable.
parts.workedSolution: An artery has a thick wall containing muscle and elastic fibres. It carries blood away from the heart at high pressure, and the thick wall withstands that pressure while the elastic fibres let it stretch and recoil with every beat. Its lumen is small. A vein has a much thinner wall with little muscle, because the blood in it is at low pressure by the time it returns, and its lumen is large. A vein also has valves, which shut if the blood starts to flow backwards, so it can only travel towards the heart. A capillary has a wall only one cell thick, so oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide have a very short distance to diffuse, and the wall is permeable, which allows materials to be exchanged with the tissues.

pattern.regex: ^(?![\s\S]*(permeable|porous|one cell thick|single cell|a cell thick|cell thick|exchange))[\s\S]*$

commonErrors.feedback: The capillary is the vessel most answers thin out. Two things earn its marks: a wall one cell thick, and a permeable wall that lets materials be exchanged with the tissues.

findTheMistake.stem:
Sinéad is asked: 'A drawing of a red blood cell is 42 mm across. The real cell is 7 µm across. Calculate the magnification. [3]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The equation in line 1 is exactly right. Line 2 divides millimetres by micrometres, which is like dividing miles by inches: the two lengths have to be in the same unit first. 42 mm is 42000 µm.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the three: the method line stands, and in a scheme that gives a mark for the equation it would be credited. The conversion mark and the answer mark go together. A useful habit is to write the unit beside every number as you substitute — the moment you see "mm ÷ µm" on the page, the conversion asks for itself.

prompts.prompt: Name the four components of blood and give the function of each.
prompts.answer: Red cells carry oxygen; white cells defend against disease; platelets convert fibrinogen to fibrin so the blood clots; plasma transports cells, food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea.

prompts.prompt: Give three adaptations of a red blood cell.
prompts.answer: Biconcave shape for a large surface area, no nucleus so there is more room inside, and packed with haemoglobin, which contains iron.

prompts.prompt: Name three substances carried in the plasma — and one that is not.
prompts.answer: Food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea are carried in the plasma. Oxygen is not: it travels inside the red blood cells.

prompts.prompt: Describe the wall of an artery and say why it is like that.
prompts.answer: Thick, with muscle and elastic fibres, to withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart and to stretch and recoil with each beat.

prompts.prompt: Describe a vein, and say what its valves do.
prompts.answer: A thin wall with little muscle and a large lumen; the valves prevent backflow, so blood at low pressure can only travel towards the heart.

prompts.prompt: Give two features of a capillary and say what each allows.
prompts.answer: Its wall is one cell thick, so substances have a short distance to diffuse, and it is permeable, so materials can be exchanged with the tissues.

prompts.prompt: Higher Tier: what happens to red blood cells put in distilled water, and why?
prompts.answer: Water enters by osmosis and they burst, because an animal cell has no cell wall to limit the entry of water. This is lysis.

prompts.prompt: How do you calculate a magnification from a drawing?
prompts.answer: Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size, with both lengths converted to the same unit first. It has no unit.
